steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on SourceP, a method that detects Ponzi schemes in Ethereum smart contracts from their source code. It should set up blockchain, Ethereum and smart contracts, explain why smart Ponzi schemes are a problem, point out the weaknesses of existing detection methods, introduce our approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Blockchain: what it is, where it is used
2. Ethereum and smart contracts
3. Turing-complete contracts, DApps, and the opening for Ponzi schemes
4. Ponzi schemes and smart Ponzi schemes: why detection matters
5. Existing detection methods and their limitations
6. Our method: SourceP
7. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Blockchain
- open ledger of transactions, distributed network of mutually untrusted peers (peer-to-peer), consensus protocol
- applications: Internet of Things, voting systems, authentication, ledgers, disaster relief, healthcare, edge computing; interest from industry and academia
- infrastructure for metaverse and Web3; DeFi, DAO, Non-Fungible Tokens increasingly popular

2. Ethereum and smart contracts
- most popular public blockchain platform with smart contract functionality
- peer-to-peer contracts via Ether (ETH); store data, run smart contracts, share info globally
- smart contracts first proposed by Nick Szabo, mid-1990s; terms auto-executed when conditions met; stored, replicated, updated in blockchain
- blockchain + smart contracts -> “peer-to-peer marketplace”, no third party between buyers and suppliers

3. Turing-completeness and DApps
- Turing-complete -> not only crypto trading but arbitrary actions on blockchain
- DApps growing fast, e.g. CryptoKitties, IDEX
- new opportunity for Ponzi schemes

4. Ponzi schemes
- 150 years old; classic fraud; promise of high profits; earlier investors/creators paid with new investors' money; no value created
- collapse when no new investors; late investors lose, scammers and early participants profit
- smart contracts: creators anonymous; immutable after deployment -> exploited on Ethereum
- = smart Ponzi schemes
- Ponzitracker: close to $3 billion in 2022, blockchain-based cryptocurrencies
- Forsage website: more than $300 million
- smart contracts are building blocks of DApps -> Ponzi contracts endanger DApps
- detecting + flagging important for preventing fraud and healthy DApps/platforms

5. Existing methods (three categories)
- bytecode/opcodes as features for classifiers or static analysis
- transaction behavior features
- opcode features + account features
- limitations: opcodes not interpretable, easy to add/remove opcodes to evade; fraudster hard to locate on anonymous Ethereum -> transaction/account features hard to collect; static analysis lags, relies on expert rules; rapid contract updates -> sustainability and performance drop
- idea: use source code instead, not considered before

6. SourceP
- pre-trained models + data flow
- pre-trained models in NLP helped many tasks -> explore for Ponzi detection
- Ethereum contracts typically in Solidity -> SourceP targets Solidity
- key innovation: only source code as feature
- flowcharts (Figure 2) compare traditional methods vs ours: no bytecode, transaction, account info -> less data, avoids too-many-features problems
- steps (Figure 4, Figure 5): source code -> data flow; code + data flow (variable dependencies) into pre-trained model; output and evaluate
- outperforms previous methods

7. Contributions
- SourceP: first to use only source code; pre-trained model for code representations + data flow semantics
- experiments: beats state-of-the-art in performance and sustainability under same conditions; good generalization
- dataset and source code released

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Blockchain technology is evolving fast. It is an open ledger of recorded transactions that is kept in a distributed network of peers that don't trust each other (i.e., a peer-to-peer network), and each peer verifies transactions through a consensus protocol. Blockchain now has applications in many areas, such as the Internet of Things, voting systems, authentication, ledgers, disaster relief, healthcare, and edge computing, and these have attracted a lot of interest from industry and academia. Blockchain has also become a common infrastructure for the emerging metaverse and Web3, and DeFi, DAO, and Non-Fungible Tokens, which were developed from blockchain technology, are getting more and more popular.

Ethereum is currently the most popular public blockchain platform that has smart contract functionality. Ethereum handles peer-to-peer contracts using the cryptocurrency Ether (ETH), and it can store data, run smart contracts, and share information globally. Smart contracts were first proposed by Nick Szabo in the mid-1990s. They contain contractual terms that are executed automatically when predefined conditions are met, and they are stored, replicated, and updated in a distributed blockchain. Putting blockchain technology and smart contracts together makes the dream of a “peer-to-peer marketplace” come true, which means that in a blockchain marketplace there is no third party intervening in transactions between buyers and suppliers that use smart contracts.

Smart contracts on Ethereum are Turing-complete, and with Turing-complete smart contracts users can not only trade cryptocurrency but also do arbitrary actions on the blockchain. Because of this, decentralized applications (DApps) made up of smart contracts are growing fast right now, for example CryptoKitties and IDEX. But at the same time smart contracts have given Ponzi schemes a new opportunity to spread.

Ponzi schemes were born 150 years ago and they are a classic financial fraud. They lure new users in by promising high profits, and the core mechanism is that the investors and creators who joined earlier are paid with the money of new investors, and the scheme itself creates no value. Once new investors stop joining, the Ponzi scheme collapses quickly, the new investors who were not compensated lose their money, and the scam makers and early participants get illegal income. With smart contracts, the creators of Ponzi schemes can stay anonymous, and since smart contracts are immutable they are extremely hard to change after they are deployed to the blockchain, and criminals exploit this feature to deploy scams on smart contract platforms like Ethereum. Ponzi schemes deployed on smart contracts like this are called smart Ponzi schemes. Ponzitracker found close to $3 billion of Ponzi schemes in 2022 that were related to blockchain-based cryptocurrencies. The recent smart Ponzi scheme event on the Forsage website involved more than $300 million. Financial fraud is so dangerous that reducing smart Ponzi schemes is urgent. Also, smart contracts are the building blocks of DApps, so if some of the smart contracts in a DApp are Ponzi schemes, then the DApp may be dangerous too. So detecting whether smart contracts deployed in Ethereum are smart Ponzi schemes and flagging them is important, to prevent financial fraud and to keep DApps and blockchain platforms developing in a healthy way.

5. Existing methods
- three categories: bytecode/opcodes (classifiers or static analysis); transaction behavior features; opcode + account features
- limitations: opcodes not interpretable and easy to evade; fraudster hard to locate -> transaction/account features hard to collect; static analysis lags, expert rules; rapid updates -> sustainability and performance drop
- use source code instead (not considered before)

6. SourceP
- pre-trained models + data flow; NLP pre-trained models helped many tasks
- Solidity
- only source code as feature; Figure 2 flowcharts: no bytecode/transaction/account info -> less data, fewer feature problems
- Figure 4, Figure 5: source code -> data flow -> pre-trained model -> output and evaluation
- outperforms previous methods

7. Contributions
- SourceP, first source-code-only method; pre-trained model + data flow
- experiments: performance, sustainability, generalization
- dataset and code released

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Blockchain technology is evolving fast. It is an open ledger of recorded transactions that is kept in a distributed network of peers that don't trust each other (i.e., a peer-to-peer network), and each peer verifies transactions through a consensus protocol. Blockchain now has applications in many areas, such as the Internet of Things, voting systems, authentication, ledgers, disaster relief, healthcare, and edge computing, and these have attracted a lot of interest from industry and academia. Blockchain has also become a common infrastructure for the emerging metaverse and Web3, and DeFi, DAO, and Non-Fungible Tokens, which were developed from blockchain technology, are getting more and more popular.

Ethereum is currently the most popular public blockchain platform that has smart contract functionality. Ethereum handles peer-to-peer contracts using the cryptocurrency Ether (ETH), and it can store data, run smart contracts, and share information globally. Smart contracts were first proposed by Nick Szabo in the mid-1990s. They contain contractual terms that are executed automatically when predefined conditions are met, and they are stored, replicated, and updated in a distributed blockchain. Putting blockchain technology and smart contracts together makes the dream of a “peer-to-peer marketplace” come true, which means that in a blockchain marketplace there is no third party intervening in transactions between buyers and suppliers that use smart contracts.

Smart contracts on Ethereum are Turing-complete, and with Turing-complete smart contracts users can not only trade cryptocurrency but also do arbitrary actions on the blockchain. Because of this, decentralized applications (DApps) made up of smart contracts are growing fast right now, for example CryptoKitties and IDEX. But at the same time smart contracts have given Ponzi schemes a new opportunity to spread.

Ponzi schemes were born 150 years ago and they are a classic financial fraud. They lure new users in by promising high profits, and the core mechanism is that the investors and creators who joined earlier are paid with the money of new investors, and the scheme itself creates no value. Once new investors stop joining, the Ponzi scheme collapses quickly, the new investors who were not compensated lose their money, and the scam makers and early participants get illegal income. With smart contracts, the creators of Ponzi schemes can stay anonymous, and since smart contracts are immutable they are extremely hard to change after they are deployed to the blockchain, and criminals exploit this feature to deploy scams on smart contract platforms like Ethereum. Ponzi schemes deployed on smart contracts like this are called smart Ponzi schemes. Ponzitracker found close to $3 billion of Ponzi schemes in 2022 that were related to blockchain-based cryptocurrencies. The recent smart Ponzi scheme event on the Forsage website involved more than $300 million. Financial fraud is so dangerous that reducing smart Ponzi schemes is urgent. Also, smart contracts are the building blocks of DApps, so if some of the smart contracts in a DApp are Ponzi schemes, then the DApp may be dangerous too. So detecting whether smart contracts deployed in Ethereum are smart Ponzi schemes and flagging them is important, to prevent financial fraud and to keep DApps and blockchain platforms developing in a healthy way.

As far as we know, the existing methods for detecting smart Ponzi schemes fall into three main categories. The first category uses bytecode or opcodes from smart contracts as features to train classifiers or do static analysis. The second category uses the transaction behavior features of smart contracts. The third category uses both opcode features and account features to train the model. But these three kinds of methods have some limitations. First, bytecode and opcode features are not interpretable, and it is easy to add or remove some opcodes in a smart contract to get around detection. Second, it is hard to locate the fraudster accurately on the anonymous Ethereum platform, so collecting the fraudster's transaction behavior characteristics and account characteristics is quite difficult. Third, static analysis methods have recognition lag and they rely on expert rules. Finally, since smart contracts are updated rapidly, the sustainability and performance of the methods available now for detecting new smart Ponzi schemes have dropped a lot. So we think about using other features to detect Ponzi schemes, such as the source code of smart contracts, which nobody has considered before.

Our Method. To deal with these challenges, we propose SourceP, a smart Ponzi scheme detection approach based on pre-trained models and data flow. Pre-trained models in current natural language processing (NLP) techniques have helped many tasks, so it makes sense to explore the great potential of pre-trained models for smart Ponzi scheme detection. Smart contracts on Ethereum are usually written in Solidity, so SourceP detects Ponzi schemes in smart contracts written in the Solidity language.

The key innovation of SourceP is that it uses only the source code of smart contracts as a feature. The flowcharts in Figure 2 show the big differences between existing traditional methods and our method for detecting smart Ponzi schemes. Comparing the two, our approach skips getting the bytecode, transaction, and account information of the smart contract, so less data is needed and the various problems of having too many features are avoided. The specific steps of SourceP are shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5. First the smart contract source code is converted into a data flow, then the source code information is fed into the pre-trained model together with the data flow that represents variable dependencies, and finally the identification results for smart contract Ponzi schemes are output and evaluated. In the end we find that SourceP does better than previous methods at smart Ponzi scheme detection.

The main contributions are as follows:

- We propose SourceP, a method to automatically detect Ponzi schemes in smart contracts. As far as we know, SourceP is the first method that detects smart Ponzi schemes using only the source code of smart contracts as features. It brings in a pre-trained model to learn code representations and uses the code semantic information from the data flow converted from the source code to do the detection.

- We did extensive experiments that show SourceP beats the state-of-the-art at detecting smart Ponzi schemes in performance and sustainability under the same conditions, and it has good generalization ability.

- We have made the dataset and source code of this study public so other researchers can replicate our methods and evaluation, to help future research in this direction.

steps.text:
Blockchain technology is evolving rapidly as an open ledger of recorded transactions maintained in a distributed network of mutually untrusted peers (i.e., a peer-to-peer network), where each peer verifies transactions through a consensus protocol [1,2,3,4]. Blockchain has now found applications in areas such as the Internet of Things [5], voting systems [6], authentication [7], ledgers [3], disaster relief [8], healthcare [9], and edge computing [10], which have attracted significant interest from industry and academia [11]. Blockchain has also become a common infrastructure for the emerging metaverse and Web3, and DeFi, DAO, and Non-Fungible Tokens developed from blockchain technology are becoming increasingly popular [12].

Ethereum [13] is currently the most popular public blockchain platform with smart contract functionality [14]. Ethereum handles peer-to-peer contracts through the cryptocurrency Ether (ETH) and can store data, run smart contracts, and share information globally. First proposed by Nick Szabo in the mid-1990s [15], smart contracts contain contractual terms that are automatically executed when predefined conditions are met, and are stored, replicated, and updated in a distributed blockchain. The combination of blockchain technology and smart contracts makes the dream of a “peer-to-peer marketplace” come true: in a blockchain marketplace, there is no third-party intervention in transactions between buyers and suppliers via smart contracts [16].

Smart contracts on the Ethereum platform are Turing-complete, and through Turing-complete smart contracts users can not only trade cryptocurrency but also perform arbitrary actions on the blockchain [17]. As a result, decentralized applications (DApps) [18,19] consisting of smart contracts, such as CryptoKitties [20] and IDEX [21], are currently growing rapidly. At the same time, however, smart contracts have given Ponzi schemes a new opportunity to spread [22].

Born 150 years ago, Ponzi schemes are a classic financial fraud that lures new users with the promise of high profits; their core mechanism is to compensate the investors and creators who joined earlier with the investments of new investors, creating no value themselves [23]. Once no new investors join, the Ponzi scheme quickly collapses: new investors who are not compensated lose their money, while the scam makers and early participants receive illegal income. Smart contracts allow the creators of Ponzi schemes to remain anonymous, and their immutability makes them extremely difficult to change once deployed to the blockchain, a feature that criminals exploit to deploy scams on smart contract platforms like Ethereum [24]. Such Ponzi schemes deployed on smart contracts are called smart Ponzi schemes. Ponzitracker [25] found close to $3 billion worth of Ponzi schemes related to blockchain-based cryptocurrencies in 2022. The recent smart Ponzi scheme event on the Forsage website involved more than $300 million [26]. The danger of financial fraud is so serious that reducing smart Ponzi schemes is urgent. Moreover, smart contracts are the building blocks of DApps, so if individual smart contracts in a DApp are Ponzi schemes, the DApp itself may also be dangerous. Detecting whether smart contracts deployed in Ethereum are smart Ponzi schemes and flagging them is therefore important to prevent financial fraud and to maintain the healthy development of DApps and blockchain platforms.

To the best of our knowledge, existing methods for detecting smart Ponzi schemes fall into three main categories: the first uses bytecode or opcodes from smart contracts as features to train classifiers or perform static analysis [27,22]; the second uses the transaction behavior features of smart contracts [28,29]; the third uses both opcode features and account features to train the model [4,30,31]. However, these methods face several limitations. First, bytecode and opcode features lack interpretability, and opcodes can easily be added to or removed from smart contracts to circumvent detection. Second, it is difficult to accurately locate the fraudster on the anonymous Ethereum platform, which makes collecting the fraudster's transaction behavior and account characteristics quite difficult. Third, static analysis methods suffer from recognition lag and rely on expert rules. Finally, with smart contracts being updated rapidly, the sustainability and performance of current methods for detecting new smart Ponzi schemes have decreased significantly. We therefore consider using other features to detect Ponzi schemes, such as smart contract source code, which no one has considered before.

Our Method. To address these challenges, we propose SourceP, a smart Ponzi scheme detection approach based on pre-trained models and data flow. Pre-trained models in current natural language processing (NLP) techniques have facilitated many tasks [32,33,34], so it is reasonable to explore their great potential in smart Ponzi scheme detection. Since smart contracts on Ethereum are typically written in Solidity [35,36], SourceP detects Ponzi schemes in smart contracts written in the Solidity language.

The key innovation of SourceP is that it uses only the source code of smart contracts as a feature. Figure 2 and Figure 2 show, through flowcharts, the significant differences between existing traditional methods and our method for detecting smart Ponzi schemes. As the comparison shows, our approach does not need to obtain the bytecode, transaction, and account information of the smart contract, which reduces the amount of data required and avoids the various problems associated with too many features. The specific implementation steps of SourceP are shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5. First, the smart contract source code is converted into a data flow; then the source code information is fed into the pre-trained model together with the data flow representing variable dependencies; finally, the identification results for smart contract Ponzi schemes are output and evaluated. Ultimately, we find that SourceP outperforms previous methods in smart Ponzi scheme detection.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

- We propose SourceP, a method to automatically detect Ponzi schemes in smart contracts. To the best of our knowledge, SourceP is the first method to detect smart Ponzi schemes using only the source code of smart contracts as features. It introduces a pre-trained model for learning code representations and uses the code semantic information provided by the data flow converted from the source code for detection.

- We conducted extensive experiments showing that SourceP outperforms the state-of-the-art in detecting smart Ponzi schemes in terms of performance and sustainability under the same conditions, and that it has good generalization ability.

- We have released the dataset and source code of this study so that other researchers can replicate our methods and evaluation, to facilitate future research in this direction.
